summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and East Nusa Tenggara stands under that national framework without any documented local deviation from it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Aceh is the only province enforcing sharia-based criminalisation.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

For East Nusa Tenggara specifically, no trans-specific statute, raid or service record exists, so no local divergence from the national baseline is documented in either direction. The province is therefore assessed at the national position: private same-sex activity is not punished, but no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections exist for sexual orientation or gender identity, and the absence of any national-level protection against discrimination is the operative baseline for a visitor in this strongly Christian-majority province.

Legal gender change on official documents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval, a requirement that applies nationwide. Sex outside marriage becomes criminalised from 2 January 2026 under the penal-code amendment passed in December 2022.

Enforcement activity documented nationally includes the arrest of three men in August 2025 over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page, with up to 12 years' imprisonment possible if convicted. Vigilante violence has also been recorded: a wave of mob attacks on trans people was reported across 14 to 16 July 2026, and The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern is uneven by province, and that unevenness matters for expectation-setting. Aceh applies religious criminal penalties that reach visitors physically present there, while South Sumatra criminalises same-sex activity under provincial provisions; the remaining provinces, East Nusa Tenggara among them, rely on national morality provisions and the new penal code rather than local religious law. A visitor moving between provinces therefore faces different exposure, though none of them carries an explicit anti-discrimination shield.

The province's strongly Christian majority distinguishes it from the Islamic legal environment of Aceh, but the sources do not show that religious composition translates into either greater tolerance or formal protection. National policy direction runs the other way: the October 2025 presidential decree places LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy, and reporting in August 2026 links that framing to vigilante attacks on transgender women.

Enforcement documented in Indonesia has been selective rather than systematic, and it has targeted gatherings and online organising as much as private conduct. The June 2025 Puncak villa raid and the August 2025 arrests over a Facebook community page both show that visibility, not only behaviour, draws state attention. The death of a trans traveler in custody in 2022 adds a custodial-risk dimension that is documented at the national level rather than in this province.
localsOnly:
Residents of East Nusa Tenggara change the gender marker on official documents only after sex-reassignment surgery and with a judge's approval. The requirement is national, and no provincial alternative or streamlined procedure is recorded in the sources.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate-crime provision covers anti-trans motivation. Recourse for a resident who is dismissed, refused service or assaulted on those grounds therefore rests on general criminal and civil law rather than on any dedicated instrument.

Residents are exposed to the penal code in force from 2 January 2026, which criminalises consensual extra-marital sex and, in the absence of same-sex marriage, reaches consensual same-sex relations. Online organising carries particular risk: three men were arrested in August 2025 over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page and face up to 12 years' imprisonment if convicted.

Vigilante violence against transgender women is documented nationally, including mob attacks across 14 to 16 July 2026 and a broader wave reported in August 2026. No province-specific incident record for East Nusa Tenggara appears in the sources, so local exposure to such attacks is not established either way.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific statute, raid, arrest or service record for East Nusa Tenggara is present in the source inventory. The absence of such documentation is unresolved rather than evidence of safety, and it is the reason the province is assessed against the national baseline instead of on its own record.

Whether the national penal code provision effective 2 January 2026 has been applied by prosecutors or courts in East Nusa Tenggara is not sourced. The same is true of local police practice toward transgender residents and visitors, and of any provincial-level guidance issued to officers.

Access to gender-affirming care, the availability of surgeons and courts able to process the sex-reassignment requirement, and the practical processing time for document changes in this province are not covered by the inventory. Nor is there sourced information on hate-crime reporting rates, since no national hate-crime provision exists to generate such data.

The claim that prosecutions under the new penal code are selective rather than systematic rests on reporting rather than on conviction statistics, and no case-level data for this province is available to test it.
